question: Explain the offence of counterfeiting under Section 178 of the BNS, including the definitions in its Explanation.
modelAnswer: Section 178 punishes whoever counterfeits, or knowingly performs any part of the process of counterfeiting, any coin, stamp issued by Government for the purpose of revenue, currency-note or bank-note, with imprisonment for life or up to ten years, and fine. Taking part in any single stage — designing, printing, stamping or finishing — is enough. The Explanation, which applies to the whole Chapter, provides: (1) a 'bank-note' is a promissory note or engagement for payment of money to bearer on demand issued by any person carrying on banking anywhere in the world, or by or under a State or Sovereign Power, and intended to be used as money; (2) 'coin' has the meaning in s.2 of the Coinage Act, 2011 and includes metal stamped and issued as money by a State; (3) causing a genuine stamp of one denomination to look like one of another is counterfeiting a Government stamp; (4) causing a genuine coin to look like a different coin, intending or knowing deception is likely, is counterfeiting coin; and (5) counterfeiting coin includes diminishing its weight or altering its composition or appearance. The offence is cognizable, non-bailable, not compoundable and triable by a Court of Session. It merges ss.231, 232, 255 and 489A IPC.

question: How has the BNS restructured the IPC provisions on coins, stamps and currency-notes?
modelAnswer: The IPC dealt with these matters in scattered provisions. Chapter XII (ss.230-263A) contained separate, parallel sections for counterfeiting coin, Indian coin, Government stamps, instruments for each, delivery, possession and use of each, and for stamp and mint offences. Currency-notes and bank-notes were covered separately by ss.489A-489E, placed among offences relating to documents and property marks. The BNS merges all of these into a single Chapter X of eleven sections (ss.178-188). Instead of one section for coins, another for stamps and a third for notes, one section now covers all four items: s.178 (counterfeiting), s.179 (using and trafficking), s.180 (possession) and s.181 (instruments and materials). The distinction between coin and 'Indian coin' disappears. The stamp-specific offences (ss.183-186) and mint offences (ss.187-188) are kept broadly as before. New features include defining 'coin' by reference to the Coinage Act, 2011, and an Explanation to s.180 exempting possession from a lawful source.

question: Distinguish between Sections 179 and 180 of the BNS.
modelAnswer: Both concern forged or counterfeit coin, stamp, currency-note or bank-note and require knowledge or reason to believe that the item is forged or counterfeit. Section 179 deals with active dealing: importing or exporting, selling or delivering, buying or receiving, otherwise trafficking in, or using as genuine. It carries imprisonment for life or up to ten years, and fine. Section 180 deals with mere possession, and adds a further mental element: the person must intend to use the item as genuine, or intend that it may be used as genuine. It carries a lighter punishment of up to seven years, or fine, or both. A new Explanation to s.180 provides that possession established to be from a lawful source is not an offence — for example, a bank official or police officer holding seized fake notes for official purposes. So a person caught paying with a fake note falls under s.179, while one found with a stock of fakes that he meant to use later falls under s.180. Both are cognizable, non-bailable and triable by a Court of Session.

question: Why does the law punish possession of counterfeiting instruments under Section 181 with the same punishment as counterfeiting itself?
modelAnswer: Section 181 punishes whoever makes or mends, or performs any part of the process of making or mending, or buys, sells, disposes of or possesses any machinery, die, instrument or material for the purpose of, or knowing or having reason to believe it is intended for, forging or counterfeiting any coin, revenue stamp, currency-note or bank-note. The punishment — life imprisonment or up to ten years, and fine — equals that for counterfeiting under s.178. This is a deliberate exception to the rule that preparation is not usually punished. Counterfeit currency threatens the whole economy: it erodes public trust in money, can fuel inflation and is used to finance organised crime and terrorism (it is expressly mentioned in s.113 on terrorist acts). Plates, dies and security paper are the source of mass production, so seizing them before fakes enter circulation is the most effective protection. Heavy punishment at the tooling stage reflects that danger. The offence is cognizable, non-bailable and triable by a Court of Session.

question: Explain Section 182 on documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes.
modelAnswer: Section 182(1) punishes whoever makes, causes to be made, uses for any purpose, or delivers to any person any document purporting to be, or in any way resembling, or so nearly resembling as to be calculated to deceive, any currency-note or bank-note, with fine up to ₹300. No intent to defraud is needed; the aim is to stop look-alikes such as advertising leaflets, toy money or wedding decorations designed like real notes, which can be passed off on the unwary. Under s.182(2), a person whose name appears on such a document who refuses, without lawful excuse, to disclose to a police officer the name and address of the printer is punishable with fine up to ₹600. Under s.182(3), a person whose name appears on the document, or on another document used or distributed with it, may be presumed, until the contrary is proved, to have caused it to be made. The offence is non-cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate — the only non-cognizable offence in the Chapter. It corresponds to s.489E IPC.

question: Discuss the offences relating to Government revenue stamps under Sections 183 to 185.
modelAnswer: These sections protect the Government's stamp revenue from reuse of stamps. Each requires that the act be done fraudulently or with intent to cause loss to the Government. Section 183 punishes removing or effacing, from any substance bearing a revenue stamp, the writing or document for which the stamp was used, or removing a used stamp from a writing or document, so that the stamp may be used for a different document — for example, chemically washing old stamp paper to resell it. The punishment is up to three years, or fine, or both. Section 184 punishes using for any purpose a revenue stamp known to have been used before, with up to two years, or fine, or both. Section 185 punishes erasing or removing from a revenue stamp the mark put on it to show that it has been used, knowingly possessing, selling or disposing of such a stamp, or selling or disposing of a stamp known to have been used, with up to three years, or fine, or both. All three are cognizable and bailable; ss.183 and 185 are triable by a Magistrate of the first class and s.184 by any Magistrate. They correspond to ss.261-263 IPC.

question: What is a 'fictitious stamp'? Explain the offences under Section 186.
modelAnswer: Under s.186(3), a 'fictitious stamp' means any stamp falsely purporting to be issued by Government to denote a rate of postage, or any facsimile, imitation or representation, whether on paper or otherwise, of any stamp issued by Government for that purpose. Section 186(1) punishes whoever (a) makes, knowingly utters, deals in or sells any fictitious stamp, or knowingly uses one for any postal purpose; (b) has a fictitious stamp in his possession without lawful excuse; or (c) makes, or has without lawful excuse, any die, plate, instrument or materials for making fictitious stamps. The punishment is fine up to ₹200. Under s.186(2), such stamps, dies, plates, instruments or materials may be seized and, if seized, are forfeited. Section 186(4) provides that for postage stamps, 'Government' in this section and in ss.178-181 and 183-185 includes persons authorised to administer executive government in any part of India or in any foreign country, so imitations of foreign postage stamps are also covered. The offence is cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate. It corresponds to s.263A IPC.

question: Explain the mint offences under Sections 187 and 188.
modelAnswer: Section 187 punishes whoever, being employed in any mint lawfully established in India, does any act, or omits what he is legally bound to do, with the intention of causing any coin issued from that mint to be of a different weight or composition from that fixed by law. The punishment is up to seven years and fine. The offender must be a mint employee, and the offence can be committed by omission — for instance, deliberately failing to carry out a required purity test. Section 188 punishes whoever, without lawful authority, takes out of any mint lawfully established in India any coining tool or instrument, with up to seven years and fine. It applies to anyone, and no intention to counterfeit need be proved; removing the tool is enough, because such tools in outside hands are an obvious counterfeiting risk. Both offences are cognizable, non-bailable, not compoundable and triable by a Magistrate of the first class. They correspond to ss.244 and 245 IPC.

question: Explain the importance of 'knowledge or reason to believe' in offences under Chapter X.
modelAnswer: Most offences in Chapter X turn on the offender's state of mind, because many people handle counterfeit money innocently. Under s.179 (using or trafficking) and s.180 (possession), the prosecution must show that the accused knew, or had reason to believe, that the coin, stamp, currency-note or bank-note was forged or counterfeit. 'Reason to believe' (defined in s.2) means he had sufficient cause to believe it, even if he did not actually know — for example, because he bought notes at far below face value, or they were obviously poor copies. Section 180 needs a further intent — to use the item as genuine or that it may be so used — and its new Explanation exempts possession from a lawful source. Section 181 requires that the tools be for counterfeiting, or known or believed to be intended for it. Counterfeiting under s.178 requires that the process be knowingly performed. In contrast, s.182 (note look-alikes) needs no guilty knowledge, and s.188 needs only that the coining tool was taken without lawful authority. A shopkeeper who unknowingly receives a fake note and passes it on in good faith commits no offence under s.179.

question: State the procedural classification of offences under Chapter X.
modelAnswer: Under the First Schedule of the BNSS: (1) ss.178 (counterfeiting), 179 (using as genuine or trafficking), 180 (possession) and 181 (instruments and materials) are cognizable, non-bailable and triable by a Court of Session. (2) s.182 (documents resembling notes) — both sub-sections (1) and (2) — is non-cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate; it is the only non-cognizable offence in the Chapter. (3) ss.183 (effacing writing or removing used stamp) and 185 (erasing used-mark) are cognizable, bailable and triable by a Magistrate of the first class, while s.184 (using a used stamp) and s.186 (fictitious stamps) are cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate. (4) ss.187 (mint employee altering coin) and 188 (taking coining instrument from mint) are cognizable, non-bailable and triable by a Magistrate of the first class. None of the offences in Chapter X is listed in BNSS s.359, so none is compoundable.

question: Problem: X buys 100 fake ₹500 notes for ₹10,000 from Y, a printer who also has the plates for making them. X spends two notes at a shop and keeps the rest at home. Z, the shopkeeper, unknowingly gives one of those notes as change to a customer. Discuss liability.
modelAnswer: Y has counterfeited currency-notes, which is an offence under s.178 (life or up to ten years and fine). His possession of the printing plates is separately punishable under s.181, and selling the fakes to X is trafficking under s.179. X bought the notes knowing, or at least with reason to believe, that they were counterfeit — buying ₹50,000 worth of notes for ₹10,000 is strong evidence of that. Buying and receiving them, and spending two as genuine, fall under s.179 (life or up to ten years). His possession of the remaining 98 notes, intending to use them as genuine, is also an offence under s.180 (up to seven years), although in practice he would be charged mainly under s.179. Z received the note in the ordinary course of business and passed it on without knowing or having reason to believe it was counterfeit; the mental element of s.179 is missing, so Z commits no offence. All of X's and Y's offences are cognizable, non-bailable and triable by a Court of Session.
